title: First or Last is Six
brief: Checks whether the number 6 is sitting at either end of the list.
description: You get a list of whole numbers. Look only at the very first spot and the very last spot in the list. If a 6 is parked in either of those two seats, return True. If neither end has a 6, return False.
solution:
def first_last6(nums):
    return nums[0] == 6 or nums[-1] == 6
hints: Python lets you grab the last item of a list with the index -1, no need to count the length.
You only need an 'or' check between two spots, not a loop over the whole list.
explainer: The solution reads index 0 and index -1 directly and combines them with or, so it returns True the instant either end equals 6.

title: Matching Ends
brief: Reports whether the list has at least one item and its first and last items match.
description: Look at a list of numbers. If the list is empty, there is nothing to compare, so return False. Otherwise compare the first item to the last item and return True only when they are equal.
solution:
def same_first_last(nums):
    return len(nums) > 0 and nums[0] == nums[-1]
hints: Check the length of the list before you try to compare anything.
A one-item list counts as matching, since its first item and last item are the same seat.
explainer: The length check guards against an empty list crashing the comparison, and the and short-circuits so nums[0] is never touched when the list is empty.

title: Build a Mini Pi
brief: Returns the fixed list [3, 1, 4], the first three digits of pi.
description: This function does not take any input. It just needs to hand back a brand new list containing the three numbers 3, 1, and 4 in that exact order, which are the first digits of the number pi.
hints: You can just write out the list directly with square brackets.
No loop or math is needed, only three numbers in order.
explainer: The function simply returns a literal list, since the task never asked it to compute anything from an input.

title: Shared End
brief: Checks whether two lists share the same first item or the same last item.
description: You get two lists of numbers, a and b. Compare their first items to each other, and separately compare their last items to each other. If either pair matches, return True. If neither pair matches, return False.
solution:
def common_end(a, b):
    return a[0] == b[0] or a[-1] == b[-1]
hints: You need two comparisons joined with or: one for the fronts, one for the backs.
Index -1 grabs the last item of each list without needing its length.
explainer: The or lets either the front pair or the back pair decide the answer, so only one side needs to line up for the result to be True.

title: Add Up Three
brief: Adds together all three numbers in a length-3 list.
description: You are given a list that always has exactly three numbers in it. Add all three of them together and return that total. The numbers can be positive, negative, or zero.
solution:
def sum3(nums):
    return nums[0] + nums[1] + nums[2]
hints: Since the list always has exactly three items, you can add them by index without a loop.
Python's built-in sum() function also works great on a whole list.
explainer: The three indexed values are simply added together, which works because the list is guaranteed to have exactly three entries.

title: Shift Left
concept: Rebuilding a list in a new order
brief: Moves the first item of a length-3 list to the end and shifts the rest left.
description: You get a list with exactly three numbers. Build and return a brand new list where the second item moves to the front, the third item moves to the middle, and the original first item moves to the last spot. The original list you were given should stay untouched.
hints: Build a new list literal using the three indexes in a different order, instead of editing nums in place.
The item that was first should end up last in the new list.
explainer: A fresh list is created by picking nums[1], nums[2], then nums[0] in that order, so the original list passed in is never changed.

title: Flip the Order
concept: Rebuilding a list in a new order
brief: Returns a length-3 list with its items in the opposite order.
description: You get a list with exactly three numbers. Build and return a brand new list where the last item comes first, the middle item stays in the middle, and the first item comes last. Do not change the list you were handed.
hints: You can build a new list by listing the indexes backwards: 2, then 1, then 0.
Python also has a slice trick, nums[::-1], that reverses a list into a new one.
explainer: A new list is assembled with nums[2] first and nums[0] last, which flips the order without touching the original list.

title: Bigger End Wins
brief: Sets both ends of a length-3 list to whichever end value was larger.
description: You get a list with exactly three numbers. Compare the first and last numbers and find the larger of the two. Return a brand new list where both the first and last spots hold that larger value, while the middle number stays exactly the same.
hints: Python's max() function can compare two numbers directly, like max(a, b).
The middle item never changes, only the two ends get replaced.
explainer: max() finds the bigger of the two end values once, then that value is placed into both the first and last slots of a fresh list.

title: Add the First Two
concept: Handling short lists as an edge case
brief: Adds up just the first two numbers in a list, or the whole list if it is shorter than that.
description: Normally this function adds only the first two numbers in the list and ignores the rest. But if the list has fewer than two numbers in it, add up whatever is there instead, including returning 0 for an empty list.
hints: Check the length of the list first to decide which path to take.
sum() on an empty list safely returns 0, which handles that edge case for you.
explainer: When the list has fewer than two items, sum() safely totals whatever is there (including nothing); otherwise only nums[0] and nums[1] are added.

title: Middle of Both
concept: Pulling one item from each of two lists
brief: Builds a new two-item list from the middle numbers of two length-3 lists.
description: You get two lists, a and b, each with exactly three numbers. Return a brand new list containing just the middle number of a followed by the middle number of b.
hints: The middle item of a length-3 list always sits at index 1.
Build the answer as a two-item list literal, one middle value from each input.
explainer: Since both lists always have three items, index 1 always points at the middle value, and those two values are packed into a new list.

title: Ends Only
concept: Picking out two items into a new list
brief: Builds a new two-item list holding just the first and last numbers of a list.
description: You get a list with at least one number in it. Return a brand new list containing only two numbers: the first item from the original list, followed by the last item from the original list.
hints: Index 0 gets the front, and index -1 gets the back, no matter how long the list is.
Pack both values straight into a new two-item list.
explainer: A new list is built from nums[0] and nums[-1] directly, which works for any list length as long as it has at least one item.

title: Hunting for 2 or 3
concept: Checking membership in two small lists
brief: Reports whether either of two length-2 lists contains a 2 or a 3.
description: You get two lists, a and b, each with exactly two numbers. Look through both lists together and return True if a 2 or a 3 shows up anywhere in either one. If neither number appears in either list, return False.
solution:
def has23(a, b):
    return 2 in a or 3 in a or 2 in b or 3 in b
hints: Python's in keyword checks whether a value is anywhere inside a list.
You need four small checks joined with or: 2 or 3, in either list.
explainer: The in operator checks each list for a 2 and for a 3, and or lets any single match anywhere make the whole result True.
